en: Homage to the one possessed of virtues, who has conquered all that is to be conquered, who shines with perfect knowledge, who constantly acts for the benefit of others, the teacher of the three worlds.
Whatever action of body, speech, or mind has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious—
"The world experiences its own fruit; there is no other agent for anything.
Thus have all the Jinas, the teachers of the three worlds, spoken out of compassion, for such indeed is the fruit of whatever action one performs.
I shall explain that in brief; it is fitting for those who seek liberation to hear it, so that they may perform actions and abandon those which cause rebirth in good and evil states.
Those men who, driven by greed, delusion, fear, and anger, are slayers of human beings—
For they kill others as well after binding them; they certainly go to Saṃjīva.
Because those who have been killed again and again come back to life there for many thousands of years, it is therefore called Saṃjīva.
Those who commit treachery against their mother, father, friends, kinsmen, or allies,
and those who speak slander and falsehoods, go to the Kālasūtra hell;
for there they are sewn together with black thread and split like pieces of wood.

Because of the blazing saws there, that hell is known as Kālasūtra. He who inflicts burning upon embodied beings with forest fires and the like is tormented by fierce flames in the Tapana hell, crying out in pain.

Because he continuously spreads an intense heat of burning, he is therefore known in the world by the name "Tapaṇa" (the Burner), which is true to its meaning. He who proclaims the perversion of dharma and adharma is an atheist (nāstika).
It causes others to suffer and it itself suffers in the Pratāpana hell.
Because it torments the beings dwelling there with a fierce fire through its excessive heat,
it is therefore called Pratāpana.
Those men who kill goats, sheep, jackals, rabbits, rats, deer, pigs, and other living beings, go to the Saṃghāta hell;
for there they are slaughtered in a mass, since their killing is carried out collectively.
Therefore, it is renowned by the name "Saṃghāta" (The Crushing Hell), a designation that accords with its meaning.
Those embodied beings who inflict physical, verbal, or mental torment upon others in this world,
and those who are cruel and deceitful, go to the Raurava hell.
Being burned there incessantly by a fierce fire, they emit a terrible roar; for that reason, it is called Raurava.
Those by whom the property of gods, brahmins, or gurus was seized here [in this world] become miserable.
Those who steal the property of others go to Mahāraurava;
for because of the fierceness of the fire's burning and the greatness of the wailing,
it is called Mahāraurava, being greater even than the great Raurava.
Having committed a grave injury against those superior in virtue,
and having slain one's mother, father, or teacher, one will certainly be cooked in the Avīci hell for an eon.
There, even the bones of embodied beings are shattered by the fierce fire.
Because there is no interval (*vīci*) of happiness therein, it is therefore called *Avīci* (the Uninterrupted).
Those who take delight in mutual malice and strike embodied beings as if in battle are born from that sin as *Asinakhās* (Sword-Clawed), partakers of suffering. (20–21)
Their very nails are swords; they are made of iron, blazing, and sharp.
Because they hack one another with them, they are known as Asinakhās (Sword-nails).
[The hell called] Lohajaṅgha consists of sixteen-finger-long thorns with blazing, sharp iron tips.
Crying out, the adulterer is forcibly made to climb a *śālmalī* tree.
(23) Large-bodied, blazing, and intensely terrifying creatures with iron fangs embrace this stealer of another's wife and devour him. (24)
Even while screaming, men who have betrayed trust are devoured by dogs, vultures, owls, and crows; in the Forest of Sword-Leaves, they are cut down again and again,
and they are made to eat glowing iron balls.

Those who steal the property of others are made to drink molten copper. Helpless and wailing, those who were always devoted to hunting are devoured by cruel dogs with iron fangs for ten million years.

Having killed fish and other aquatic creatures, a man goes to the Vaitaraṇī river, whose waters are molten, glowing copper; there he is constantly burned by fire. He who, deluded by a mere fragment of self-interest, engages in unrighteous legal proceedings...
He who cries out in hell is crushed by a wheel.
Whatever kinds of torment were inflicted upon embodied beings here [in this world], they are tormented for a long time by those same heated machines, mountains, and hammers. (29–30)
Those men who are destroyers of the bridges of dharma and proponents of false paths, having entered the path strewn with razor edges, they traverse it;
having crushed lice and other insects with their nails, they are themselves crushed by mountains of wool.
Again and again, those large-bodied ones wail for a hundred autumns.
But he who, having undertaken a vow, does not properly observe it,
will surely be cooked in the *kukūla* fire with his flesh and bones wasting away.
For whoever lives by even a slight wrong livelihood is devoured by fierce worms while submerged in the mud of excrement.
Those who grind to powder living beings found even within grains of rice—
They are repeatedly agitated by glowing iron pestles.
Those who were exceedingly wrathful, cruel, deceitful, and desirous of evil,
and who rejoiced in the misfortunes of others, are born as the rākṣasas of Yama.
One should avoid even the slightest evil of body, speech, and mind— whether it be of the mild or other degrees— for that is the seed of all sufferings. [The Section on Hell is completed.]
Through passion for their wombs, even swans, pigeons, and other such creatures, though they possess harsh voices, are born as deluded insects and the like;
through anger and malice, they become serpents; and through pride, they become the stiff-necked lords of beasts.
Through arrogance, embodied beings are born in the wombs of donkeys, dogs, and the like;
through defects such as envy and jealousy, they are born after death as monkeys—
talkative, audacious, and fickle-natured— and as crows.
Through acts of killing, binding, and envy toward cows, horses, and other embodied beings, those of cruel deeds are born as spiders,
scorpions, and locusts; [as well as] tigers, cats, jackals, bears, vultures, wolves, and the like.
After death, men who are wrathful and envious are born as meat-eaters.
Wrathful and cruel men become highly powerful *nāgas* through their generosity;
yet through pride and anger, they become lords of the *garuḍas*.

Whatever evil deed has been committed by oneself through speech, body, or mind, by that one is born as an animal; therefore, do not commit even the slightest of such acts. [The section on animals is completed.]
Those base ones who steal food and drink, being devoid of charity,
become *kaṭapūtana* pretas who feed upon corpses.
Those who harass children and deceive them out of greed [become likewise].
Those who feed on the impurities of the womb are born as kaṭapūtanas.
Those men who, having died, are of base conduct, exceedingly wretched, envious, and ever-covetous, are born as pretas with goiters on their necks.

He who obstructs the giving of gifts and does not give anything at all shall become a hungry ghost with a vast belly and a needle-like mouth, tormented by hunger. He who guards his wealth for the sake of his lineage, neither consuming it nor giving it away, [shall likewise suffer].
Then that deceased person is born as a ghost who takes what has been given.
He who desires to seize the property of others and yet feels remorse after giving it away is born as a ghost after death who eats excrement, phlegm, and vomit.
He who, out of anger, speaks unpleasant words that strike at the vital points and pierce the very core of others,
becomes a *ulkāmukha* preta for a very long time because of that deed.
He who, merciless and cruel-minded, incites strife, eats worms,
insects, and moths, and becomes a *preta*, shall become a *jyotika*.
He who is a village usurer gives gifts while also causing oppression.

One who is cruel and gives food for the sake of killing living beings is born as a Kumbhāṇḍa, a being of deformed appearance, even while being honored. Those who kill living beings mercilessly for the sake of their own food will certainly become Rākṣasas after death and receive various kinds of edible foods.
Those who are always devoted to perfumes and garlands, who have little anger, and who are generous,
are born after death as Gandharvas, serving as sources of delight for the gods.
Some who are wrathful and slanderous give gifts only for the sake of wealth.
That evil-minded person is born as a Piśāca with a deformed face.
Men who are constantly wicked, fickle, and harmful to others,
yet always delight in giving, become Pretas after death.
Those who are cruel, wrathful, yet generous, and who are fond of wine and liquor,
are born after death as yakṣas— cruel-souled beings who are lovers of liquor.
Those who carry their mothers, fathers, and teachers in vehicles wherever they desire, [are born as gods].
Those endowed with happiness are born as yakṣas who travel in celestial chariots.
Due to the fault of craving and envy, these beings—yakṣas and the like—become hungry ghosts after death; therefore, one should avoid them because they are afflicted by impurities.
[The Pretakāṇḍa is completed.
Among gods, asuras, and humans, long life arises from non-violence;
indeed, through violence one is born with a short life. Therefore, one should avoid violence. (61)
Leprosy, consumption, fever, insanity, and whatever other diseases afflict men arise from having committed acts of killing, binding, or beating toward living beings.
For he who seizes the property of others and gives nothing in return [suffers these consequences].
Even with great effort, he does not acquire wealth.
He who takes wealth that has not been given and bestows it as gifts becomes wealthy after death, only to become poor once again.
That man who is neither a thief nor a giver, yet is not excessively miserly,
will certainly obtain wealth that is stable even with great difficulty.
He who does not seize the property of others, who is generous, and free from envy— [he attains such wealth].
That man obtains vast and imperishable wealth that is desired;
endowed with long life, complexion, and strength, illustrious and free from disease, he shall always be happy—he who gives food here in this world. (66–67)
Modest, handsome, an enjoyer of pleasures, possessing a beautiful complexion, and dear to all living beings—
he who gives garments shall obtain fine clothes. He who gives a dwelling here with a very serene mind [attains the same].
Palaces and all objects of desire arise for that embodied being.
Those men who give sandals, bridges, and the like,
always become happy and obtain vehicles.
Having caused water-reservoirs such as wells, pits, and ponds to be constructed,
they become happy, freed from distress, and free from thirst.
Adorned with flowers, glorious, and a refuge for all embodied beings—
He who bestows a grove shall always be prosperous.
Through the gift of knowledge, scholarship is attained; through the practice of wisdom, it is likewise achieved. By the gift of medicine and the gift of fearlessness, one is born free from disease.
By the gift of lamps one becomes possessed of vision; by the gift of musical instruments, one possesses a beautiful voice;
by the gift of beds and seats, a person becomes happy.
He who gives cows and other such animals here, as well as food accompanied by milk, [attains great merit].
That man shall be powerful, possessed of a fine complexion, an enjoyer of pleasures, and long-lived.
By the gift of a daughter in marriage, he shall obtain his desires and possess a large retinue.
One who is abundant in wealth and grain is born through the gift of land.
Leaves, flowers, fruit, water, the granting of safety, and pleasant speech—
whatever is desired should be given with devotion to the seeker of it.

He who gives here after having caused affliction—whether for the sake of heaven, out of fear, or from a desire for fame and pleasure—obtains an afflicted fruit. But he who gives with a mind permeated by compassion, regardless of his own interest, [attains a pure fruit]. (78)
He who gives here for the sake of others enjoys an unafflicted fruit.
Whatever is given to another at the proper time and according to the rule, all that returns to him in that very same manner. (79–80)
Without harming others, at the proper time, according to one's desire,
and without causing them distress, one should give that which is beneficial and not contrary to the Dharma.
For it is only in this manner that the fruit of a gift being given arises.
For charity is considered the sole cause of all happiness.
One who abstains from the wives of others will obtain beloved wives; by avoiding even one's own wife at improper places or times, one attains virility. (82–83)

That man who does not restrain a mind attached to the wives of others, and who takes delight in improper objects, attains womanhood. But she who detests womanhood, being well-behaved and of little passion, [attains manhood]. (84)
That woman who constantly desires manhood shall attain the state of a man.
But he who properly practices the fearless life of celibacy (brahmacarya) becomes radiant, endowed with excellent qualities, and glorious; he is honored even by the gods.
By abstaining from the consumption of intoxicants, a person becomes firm in mindfulness, free from delusion,
truthful in speech, and endowed with fame and happiness. He who does not create division even among beings who are already divided—
He becomes one whose retinue is indivisible and whose mind is steadfast.
That man who always carries out the commands of his gurus with a joyful heart,
and who speaks of what is beneficial and harmful, shall have speech that is accepted by others.
The base, by means of insulting others and through perversion, rise up;
they become happy by giving happiness, and miserable by giving misery.
Delighting in the deceptions of others, they are deceitful and speakers of untruth.
Those who are conceited about their physical appearance become hunchbacked and dwarfish.
One becomes dull-witted through envy of knowledge, and one who cherishes likes and dislikes becomes mute.
A foolish soul who finds fault with beneficial advice suffers from deafness.
Suffering results from evil, happiness from merit, and a mixture from mixed actions; all is a flow corresponding [to its cause], for the fruit of karma is inconceivable. (93)
[The Chapter on Humans is completed.
He who always acts with guile and deceit, yet remains free from committed sin, who is fond of strife and is generous, shall become a lord of the Asuras. (94)
[The Section on Asuras is completed.
He who does not desire happiness for himself and does not rejoice in possessions—he, the foremost of the planets, shall attain the state of a Mahārājika. 95
One who honors his mother, father, and elders, who is generous and patient,
and who does not rejoice in quarrels, is born among the thirty gods.
They take no delight in conflict, nor do they have minds that rejoice in strife.
Those who are exclusively devoted to what is wholesome and have approached the Yāma heaven;
those who are learned, upholders of the Dharma, possessed of excellent wisdom, and desirous of liberation;
and those men who are gladdened by their virtues—they are the ones who have approached the Tuṣita heaven.

Those men who themselves engage in the discipline of the gift of ethical conduct and possess great enthusiasm will certainly go to the Nirmāṇarati heaven. Those excellent beings who are not dejected in spirit through their generosity, self-control, and restraint [will likewise attain that state].
And those who possess superior virtues certainly go to the realm of Paranirmita.
Through ethical conduct one attains heaven, and through meditative concentration especially;
through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, there is ultimately no further rebirth.
This action, which has been clearly explained as having both auspicious and inauspicious fruits:
through the auspicious, happiness is obtained, while suffering arises from the inauspicious.
Death, disease, and old age—these three must be kept in mind.
Separation from beloved ones and the fruit of one's own past actions—by reflecting thus, one attains detachment;
being detached, one attains merit and likewise avoids sin. Listen now to this in brief. (103–104)

Properly accomplishing the welfare of others and avoiding harm to others is merit; the opposite of this is said by the Great-Souled One to be sin. (105) The *Ṣaḍgatikārikā* composed by the great scholar Aśvaghoṣa, extracted from the *Āryasaddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-mahāyāna-sūtrānta*, is hereby completed.
